extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, and patent attorneys working on software and AI-related patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and drafting software and AI patent claims to satisfy the Alice/Mayo §101 patent-eligibility framework, using USPTO AI guidance and Federal Circuit case law to avoid abstract-idea rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step test
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-step process from the Supreme Court (Alice/Mayo) used to assess patent subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Step 1: determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (e.g., an abstract idea). Step 2: if so, determine whether the claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, add an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent attorneys must analyze inventions thoroughly using this two-step framework. The test is central to determining whether software/AI inventions are too abstract to be patented; examiners and courts may apply it differently, and district courts often conduct independent eligibility analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of abstract ideas (USPTO AI guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO identifies three main categories of abstract ideas that commonly appear in AI claims: (1) Mathematical concepts (relationships, formulas, equations, calculations); (2) Methods of organizing human activity (business methods, workflows); (3) Mental processes (observations, evaluations, judgments that could in theory be done in the human mind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims 'don’t include mental processes' when they contain limitations that can't practically be performed in the human mind; AI claims that simply rely on mathematical principles but don't recite formulas in claim language can sometimes be argued not to 'recite' a mathematical concept. Use this categorization to identify the exception implicated and to craft claims that avoid explicit recitation of abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: reciting vs. involving an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO distinguishes claims that explicitly 'recite' an abstract idea (triggering further eligibility analysis) from claims that merely involve or base themselves on an abstract idea without reciting it in the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to avoid explicit recitation of abstract ideas where possible; emphasize concrete claim language showing technological implementation or limitations. This distinction affects whether a claim is treated as containing a judicial exception for Alice/Mayo analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement (Alice Step Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step Two, the claim must contain an 'inventive concept' — additional elements that transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application by providing something significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show specific technical progress (improvements to computer operation or other technology), and avoid relying on elements that are common, ordinary, or conventional. The patent specification should clearly state a distinct technical challenge and its solution to support the inventive concept. For AI inventions, emphasize technological advances rather than broad applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply adding a basic computer or generic computer implementation to a claim does not supply an inventive concept and won't make an abstract idea patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claims that only invoke generic computer components or routine computer activities (e.g., storing information in a database) without specifying how those components are specially configured or achieve a technological improvement. Courts and examiners view such generic implementations as non-inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant post-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-solution activities that are routine or conventional (e.g., basic data gathering or common computation) do not meaningfully add inventiveness to a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on trivial follow-up steps after an abstract computation to supply the inventive concept. Instead, include novel or creative components and demonstrate how claimed post-solution steps materially contribute to a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application integration ('technological solution to a technological problem')
rubrics_metrics.description: An otherwise abstract idea can be patent-eligible if the claim integrates the abstract idea into a practical application that meaningfully limits it and shows a concrete technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the claim as a whole applies the abstract idea within a technical environment (e.g., network monitoring with remedial blocking actions, improved speech-transcription pipeline, or specific treatment protocols following AI diagnosis). Use claim elements that show how computing/technology is improved or how the abstract idea is functionally integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO AI Example 1 — Anomaly detection in network security (Examples 47-49 synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO Example: An ANN that detects anomalies in network security produced three analyzed claims: Claim 1 (eligible) — apparatus claim for an application-specific integrated circuit implementing the ANN; Claim 2 (ineligible) — method merely leveraging ANN to identify anomalies; Claim 3 (eligible) — method integrating anomaly detection within network monitoring plus remedial blocking actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lessons: prefer concrete machine/device claims or include practical, domain-specific follow-up actions that materially change system behavior. Merely claiming use of an ANN to analyze data without field-of-use or actionability risks ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO AI Example 2 — Speech separation with DNNs
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO Example: Broad method of applying DNNs to separate voices (Claim 1) is ineligible as it recites abstract mathematical analysis. Claims that specify application context (improving transcription accuracy, generating enhanced audio outputs) are eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie signal-processing/AI methods to downstream technological benefits (e.g., clearer audio, better transcription) and concrete improvements in performance or functionality rather than claiming bare mathematical transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO AI Example 3 — AI in medical diagnosis and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO Example: An AI algorithm identifying disease from data (diagnosis) can be ineligible if treated as abstract data analysis or natural law; claims become eligible when linked to specific treatment steps (administering therapy) that transform insight into practical therapeutic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In medical AI, include intervention or concrete treatment steps or otherwise tie discoveries to applied protocols to avoid Mayo-style natural-law exclusions. Pure diagnostic correlations are vulnerable to rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test as a helpful (but not sole) tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test checks whether a process is tied to a particular machine or transforms an article into a different state; while useful, it is not the exclusive test for process patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use machine-or-transformation factors to support eligibility arguments where appropriate (e.g., claim a specific machine implementation or a substantive transformation), but don't treat passing this test as automatically dispositive under Alice/Mayo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical improvement examples that indicate inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete technical improvements that can support eligibility include: better computer vision solving previously unsolvable problems; more efficient data processing reducing computational overhead; increased speed or accuracy in ML operations; novel neural network architectures addressing technical limitations; reduced resource requirements; improved handling of noisy/incomplete/corrupted data sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, quantify or specifically describe the technical benefit (reduction in computational load, accuracy gains, resource savings) in the specification and claims to demonstrate an inventive concept beyond abstract computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly broad claim drafting and emphasize specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are overly broad or mirror categories frequently rejected by USPTO are at high risk under Alice/Mayo. Drafting should emphasize specific technical features and concrete effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft multiple independent claims covering different practical applications and specific technical elements; document incremental improvements in the specification; avoid generic language and broad functional claiming that merely recites high-level goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with examiners and use prosecution strategy (continuations, appeals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proactive engagement with USPTO examiners, considered use of continuation applications, and strategic appeals can improve outcomes when facing Alice rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain technical specifics to examiners, correct other rejection categories before appealing when helpful, and consider continuation practice to adapt claim scope to evolving case law and guidance. Thompson Patent Law reports these strategies can materially shorten prosecution time and increase allowance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Circuit and case-law constraints (e.g., Recentive Analytics v. Fox)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent Federal Circuit decisions reinforce that simply applying conventional machine learning algorithms to new data environments is not a patent-eligible inventive concept; courts demand demonstration of technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing eligibility, address relevant Federal Circuit precedent head-on and show how claim elements provide a technological improvement beyond applying standard ML techniques to a dataset. Use case law to craft contrasts between conventional application and claimed innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims not performable in the human mind can avoid 'mental processes' exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO notes that claims including limitations that cannot practically be performed mentally (e.g., massive dataset calculations, complex computations) are less likely to be treated as reciting a mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize computational scale, data volumes, or operations infeasible for humans in claim and specification language to help distinguish claims from mental-process judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner-of-invention (use of AI) doesn't change eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO states that how an invention was made (including via AI) does not affect subject-matter eligibility — examiners evaluate claims based on claim content and the improvements they recite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on the fact that AI assisted invention; instead, focus on drafting claim language that recites specific technical improvements. Also be mindful of prior-art issues from AI-generated outputs as potential novelty/non-obviousness challenges.
